newsitem.title: JAPAN: Reuters survey of Asian nuclear power plans.
newsitem.headline: Reuters survey of Asian nuclear power plans.

text.p: Following is a survey of nuclear energy plans in Asia on a country-by-country basis.

Capacity addition assessments are from Japan's Institute of Energy Economics. Monetary assessments are based on analyst views pegging the construction cost of one megawatt of capacity at $2 million to $3 million. The costs include those of plants already under construction. A gigawatt is equal to one million watts.
-- Intense public scrutiny Japan's nuclear program because of a series of accidents and failed cover-ups.
-- Plans to build an additional 20 to 25 GW by the 2010.
-- Plans to build some 28 new plants totalling 26.3 GW of new capacity by 2010.
-- Currently operates 5.1 GW of capacity and plans to add 2.6 GW of new capacity by 2010.

Note: Taiwan has been embroiled in fierce debate over nuclear policy for the last year, with a deeply divided parliament voting last October to restore funding for a $4.1 billion plant and sparking one of the worst political riots to mar the island's fledgling democracy.
-- Currently operates just one facility with 140 megawatts (MW) of capacity.
-- Currently operates 1.84 GW. Plans an additional 5.76 GW.
-- India's detonation of a nuclear device in 1974 made the country ineligible to receive new Western technologies.
-- Unveiled plans Friday for the construction of its first experimental reactor.
-- The 10 MG research reactor will be located 60 kilometres north of Bangkok.
-- No plans for nuclear power until 2022, and even then nuclear power will still represent less than one percent of the country's projected 87.8 GW total electricity generation capacity.
-- A 620 MW nuclear facility was built in Batan, north of Manila, in the 1980s but was never commissioned due to a legal battle between the government and the builders of the plant.
-- Government has decided to convert the plant into a 1,500 MG gas-fired facility.
-- The country's plan for its first nuclear power plant, to be completed by 2003 at a cost of $7 billion, was pushed back in March for another 20 to 30 years.

-- The United States forged a pact with Pyongyang in 1994 and North Korea froze its old-style graphite-moderated civil nuclear programme. In return, a consortium of states, including South Korea and Japan, agreed to pay for the construction of safer, light water reactors, which produce little plutonium.
-- The government says it is aiming to establish a nuclear power industry, but the the first plants are not expected to be operating before 2010.
